l: exile of the Zoramite believers, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Those who favored the words preached by Alma and his brethren were cast out of the land, and many came to the land of Jershon. The Zoramites who were brought to repentance were also driven out and received lands for their inheritance in Jershon.

l: holy angel, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A holy angel sent by God stops Alma and the sons of Mosiah as they seek to destroy the church, warning Alma with a thunder-like voice.

l: promised land, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Promised land is a place reached by forefathers and entered by fathers through God's power, guided straight by the Liahona.

l: Alma's conversion, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Alma’s conversion began when an angel stopped his destruction of God’s church; after three days of suffering, he called on Jesus Christ, received joy and light, was born of God, and brought souls to repentance.

l: workers of darkness and secret combinations, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Workers of darkness and secret combinations commit murders and wickedness, are cursed, and face destruction unless they repent before fully ripe.

l: land, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Land bears God’s blessing for the righteous and is possessed by Nephi’s people, where Helaman and his brethren establish churches; it is cursed for workers of darkness and secret combinations, and unto destruction for every wicked nation, kindred, tongue, and people when fully ripe.

l: plates of Nephi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The plates of Nephi contain records that are to be kept and preserved as sacred. They are part of the records entrusted to Helaman.

l: plates of brass, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The plates of brass contain engravings, holy scriptures, mysteries, and forefathers’ genealogy; kept bright, they are preserved by God and handed down until reaching every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.

l: twenty-four plates, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Twenty-four plates are kept to reveal a destroyed people’s mysteries, darkness, secret works, murders, robbings, plunderings, wickedness, and abominations.

l: interpreters, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: are_preserved preserved [by Helaman] The interpreters were prepared so that the word of God concerning the secret works and abominations of a destroyed people could be fulfilled. Helaman is commanded to preserve them.

l: Liahona, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Liahona is a compass, ball, or director prepared by God to show the course through the wilderness; it works according to faith, but its marvelous works cease when people are slothful and fail to exercise faith and diligence.

l: word of Christ, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The word of Christ points people on a straight course to eternal bliss, carrying those who follow beyond the vale of sorrow into a far better promised land.

l: mysteries, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The mysteries are not yet fully made known to Helaman's father. They are preserved for a wise purpose known to God.

l: works of darkness, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The secret works of a destroyed people, including their murders, robbings, plunderings, wickedness, and abominations, are to be made known to the people. Their oaths, covenants, agreements, signs, and wonders are to be kept from the people.

l: secret plans, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Secret plans involving oaths, covenants, and agreements of workers of darkness must be withheld so people avoid darkness and destruction; instead, people should hate sin and iniquity and learn that wicked murderers were destroyed.

l: destruction of the wicked, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The wicked workers of darkness and secret combinations were destroyed after they failed to repent. The land is cursed to destruction for such workers unless they repent before they are fully ripe.

l: word of truth and righteousness, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_spoken_by Lord Jesus Christ The word of truth and righteousness is identified with Christ, who is also described as the life and light of the world.

l: Isabel, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Isabel, a harlot who steals many hearts, draws the son into Siron among the Lamanite borders.

l: ministry, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a calling [to declare glad tidings unto the people and prepare their minds] The son was entrusted with a ministry to declare glad tidings to the people and prepare their minds for the coming of Christ. He forsook this ministry when he went after Isabel.

l: resurrection of Christ, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The resurrection of Christ marks the point up to which the first resurrection includes the righteous from Adam’s days, making possible the reunion and restoration of soul, body, and every bodily part.

l: first resurrection, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: First resurrection reunites souls and bodies of those from Adam to Christ, including the righteous before those who die after Christ’s resurrection; it is not merely consigning souls to happiness or misery.

l: reuniting of soul and body, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: occurs resurrection of Christ [possibly at Christ's resurrection and ascension] The reuniting of soul and body occurs at resurrection. It restores every limb, joint, and even every hair to its proper and perfect frame.

l: paradise, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A state of happiness, rest, and peace where righteous spirits rest from trouble, care, and sorrow before resurrection.

l: endless night of darkness, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a state of misery [for the wicked] Outer darkness is the state to which the spirits of the wicked are cast. It includes weeping, wailing, gnashing of teeth, and fearful expectation of God's wrath.

l: restoration, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Restoration reunites soul and body, restoring every limb, joint, and hair to a proper, perfect frame and fulfilling what the prophets have spoken. Required by the justice of God, it returns all things to proper order, bringing like for like: righteousness, justice, and mercy for their corresponding qualities, but evil, carnal, and devilish things for the same. It condemns rather than justifies the sinner.

l: appointed time, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: determines resurrection [when all shall rise from the dead] God has appointed a time when all shall come forth from the dead, though no one among men knows when it will be. The appointed time includes the resurrection and the end of the interim states of happiness and misery.

l: space between death and resurrection, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: There is a space between death and the resurrection of the body. During this space, souls remain in paradise or outer darkness until God appoints the time for them to come forth.

l: the speaker's son, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The speaker's son, a sinner, is taught restoration, justice, the fall, repentance, mercy, and the atonement. Warned against further offense, he is urged to be merciful, just, righteous, and continually good, then called of God to preach truthfully and bring souls to repentance.

l: works, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: are_good good [in this life] They determine what men are restored to at the last day. Good works result in restoration to good, while evil works result in restoration to evil.

l: desires of the heart, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: are_good good They are considered with works in determining what men are restored to at the last day.

l: misery, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a state [of the sinner cut off from God's presence] It is the endless result for those restored to evil and who inherit the kingdom of the devil.

l: sin, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Sin requires law, survives restoration into happiness, and brings remorse and justice’s claims; the speaker urges his son to repent and commit no further sin.

l: state of nature, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Those in it, or in a carnal state, are in the gall of bitterness and bonds of iniquity, without God in the world.

l: nature of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Men in a carnal state have gone contrary to it.

l: nature of happiness, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Those in a carnal state are in a state contrary to it.

l: spiritual death, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_reclaimed_by the plan of redemption [because the soul could never die] Spiritual death is being cut off from the presence of the Lord. The plan of redemption provides a means for mankind to be reclaimed from it.

l: the plan of happiness, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_destroyed_by reclaiming mankind from temporal death The plan of happiness is described as eternal as the life of the soul. Reclaiming man from temporal death would destroy it.

l: the plan of mercy, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The plan of mercy requires the atonement, claims the penitent through it, and thereby appeases justice’s demands.

l: punishment, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Punishment is eternal, affixed to the law and opposite the plan of happiness; justice executes it when claiming the sinner, enabling repentance.

l: Zerahemnah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Zerahemnah is a Lamanite chief leader and commander who appoints Amalekites and Zoramites as captains, stirs anger against the Nephites, and seeks power over both peoples. Armed for war, he leads forces that are surrounded by Moroni’s and Lehi’s armies. He refuses an oath, attacks Moroni and is wounded, urges further fighting, then promises a covenant of peace to spare surviving Lamanites.

l: defense of families and lands, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The Nephites contend to defend their families, lands, country, rights, and religion. The Lord has said that they should defend their families even unto bloodshed.

l: conflict, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Moroni says the conflict will end if the Lamanites accept his conditions. When Zerahemnah refuses, the conflict continues until the Lamanites are being destroyed.

l: covenant of peace, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: requires weapons of war [to be surrendered before departure] Many Lamanites enter into a covenant of peace and are allowed to depart into the wilderness. Zerahemnah later promises that he and his people will make the same covenant if the remaining Lamanites are spared.

l: death of the combatants, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is exceedingly great [among both Nephites and Lamanites] Many Nephites and Lamanites die, and the number of dead is not counted because it is exceedingly great. Their bodies are cast into the waters of Sidon and buried in the depths of the sea.

l: scalp of Zerahemnah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Zerahemnah’s chief’s scalp is removed by a Nephite soldier, raised on a sword as a warning of death, frightening many Lamanites into surrendering.

l: prophecy, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Alma's prophecy, written by Helaman and withheld until fulfilled, foretells the people of Nephi's unbelief, destruction, decline, extinction, and the fate of survivors.

l: unbelief, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: causes people of Nephi [their decline and extinction] Alma prophesies that the people of Nephi will dwindle in unbelief four hundred years after Jesus Christ manifests himself to them. Their unbelief will lead them into darkness, lasciviousness, and iniquities.

l: dissensions, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: endanger Nephites [despite their victory and deliverance] Dissensions arise when people refuse to hearken to Helaman and his brethren and are led by Amalickiah’s flatteries. They make the affairs of the Nephites precarious and dangerous and cause Moroni to gather forces against Amalickiah.

l: Amalickiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Amalickiah is a large, strong, subtle, evil Nephite by birth who desires kingship. Through flattery, cunning, fraud, and deceit, he leads people into dissension and wickedness, seeking to destroy the church of God and the foundation of liberty. Opposed by Moroni, he flees to the land of Nephi, stirs the Lamanites against the Nephites, gains command of their armies, poisons Lehonti, arranges the Lamanite king’s assassination, marries the queen, and obtains the Lamanite kingdom. As king, he hardens the Lamanites, gathers a large army, seeks dominion over the land and bondage for the Nephites, and wages war with vengeance against Moroni. His forces capture Nephite cities, including the city of Moroni. After being angered by losses and swearing to drink Moroni’s blood, he continues leading the Lamanite army until Teancum kills him with a javelin.

l: Amalickiahites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Dissenting Nephites supporting Amalickiah seek power, are captured and returned to Zarahemla; those rejecting a free-government covenant are executed.

l: Christians, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Christians are true believers in Christ who belong to the church of God, gladly take Christ’s name, and are prayed for to be favored with their cause and freedom.

l: chosen land, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is land of liberty [all the land north and south of the land Desolation] Moroni names all the land south of the land Desolation, and ultimately all the land on the north and south, a chosen land.

l: land of liberty, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is chosen land [all the land north and south of the land Desolation] Moroni names the land a land of liberty and teaches that God will not allow the people who take upon themselves the name of Christ to be destroyed until their own transgressions bring it upon them.

l: title of liberty, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The title of liberty is a standard made from a rent part of Moroni’s coat, bearing words concerning God, religion, freedom, peace, wives, and children. Moroni raises it before the people; it is then hoisted across Nephite towers, including by king-men compelled to defend their country.

l: covenant of freedom, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The covenant of freedom, made by Nephites to keep peace and not forsake the Lord, supports freedom and free government; few refuse and are put to death.

l: march against Amalickiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Moroni takes his gathered and armed army into the wilderness to cut off Amalickiah’s course. He heads Amalickiah’s armies, causing Amalickiah to flee and the remainder of his men to be delivered into Moroni’s hands.

l: peace in the land, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_maintained Nephites [until nearly the end of the nineteenth year of the reign of the judges] Peace returns to the land after Moroni establishes the standard of liberty among the Nephites. The people maintain peace until nearly the end of the nineteenth year of the reign of the judges.

l: religion, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_maintained_by Christians [through the covenant] The people covenant to maintain their religion along with their rights. Amalickiah seeks to destroy the religion of the church of God, while Moroni’s title of liberty calls the people to preserve it.

l: Lehonti, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Lehonti leads Lamanites who refuse to fight the Nephites and gathers them on mount Antipas, joins Amalickiah as second leader, then dies after Amalickiah administers poison by degrees.

l: queen, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The queen receives Amalickiah’s message about the king’s death and asks him to spare the city’s people and provide witnesses. Amalickiah wins her favor, marries her, and thereby obtains the kingdom.

l: servants of the king, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Servants of the Lamanite king flee after his stabbing, escape false accusation, cross into Zarahemla, and join the people of Ammon.

l: armies of Lehonti, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: are_led_by Lehonti The armies of Lehonti surround Amalickiah’s men before dawn after Lehonti agrees to Amalickiah’s plan. They receive Amalickiah’s men after those men plead to join them.

l: army of Amalickiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_commanded_by Amalickiah [under the king’s command] The army of Amalickiah camps near mount Antipas and is initially commanded to compel the disobedient Lamanites to arms. It is surrounded by Lehonti’s armies, joins with them, and later marches with Amalickiah to the land of Nephi and the city of Nephi.

l: mount Antipas, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: contains armies of Lehonti [on its top] Mount Antipas is where the Lamanites who resist the king gather in preparation for battle. Amalickiah camps in the nearby valley and uses secret messages to negotiate with Lehonti.

l: proclamation, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: calls_for battle against the Nephites [throughout all the king’s land] The proclamation is sent throughout the Lamanite land by the king, commanding the people to gather again for battle against the Nephites. Most of the people refuse to obey it because they fear losing their lives.

l: dethroning the king, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_intended_by Amalickiah [as a plan] Dethroning the king is Amalickiah’s intention from the beginning of his command over the Lamanite army. He accomplishes it by gaining control of the armies and arranging the king’s assassination.

l: death of Lehonti, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The death of Lehonti is caused by poison that Amalickiah has one of his servants administer by degrees. After Lehonti dies, the Lamanites appoint Amalickiah as their leader and chief commander.

l: king murdered by Amalickiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_committed_by servants of Amalickiah [by stabbing the king to the heart] The assassination of the king occurs when one of Amalickiah’s servants stabs him to the heart while appearing to honor him. Amalickiah then uses fraud to accuse the king’s servants and gain the people’s support.

l: marriage of Amalickiah and the queen, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: makes Amalickiah [a means of obtaining the kingdom] The marriage of Amalickiah and the queen helps Amalickiah obtain the kingdom. After the marriage, he is acknowledged as king throughout the land among the Lamanites and related groups.

l: fraud, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: helps Amalickiah [in gaining the hearts of the people and obtaining the kingdom] Fraud enables Amalickiah to gain the hearts of the people after the king’s assassination. Through fraud and the assistance of his cunning servants, he obtains the kingdom.

l: land, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Land inhabited by Nephites and Lamanites is fortified across cities and borders as Amalickiah seeks rule over it.

l: fortifications, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Fortifications protect armies, especially where land requires more men, by enclosing forces along the Nephite-Lamanite line.

l: chief captains, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Lamanite chief captains lead attacks against Nephite cities, swear to destroy them, doubt success because of wickedness, and are slain after failed assaults on Ammonihah and Noah.

l: city of Noah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Noah, once weak, is fortified by Moroni under Lehi, exceeds Ammonihah’s strength, and defeats Lamanites attacking its entrance.

l: Nephite army, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: defends city of Ammonihah [from the Lamanites] The Nephite army was stationed by the borders of Ammonihah to defend the city. Its preparations helped prevent the Lamanites from taking the city.

l: places of security, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Forts of security were built or fortified for city defenses, with high banks, deep ditches, and guarded sole entrances restricting access to designated passes.

l: city defenses, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: City defenses combined raised banks, deep ditches, and weapons, giving the Nephites power over attacking Lamanites.

l: Lamanite attack on Ammonihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_defeated_by Nephites [through fortified defenses] The Lamanite attack on Ammonihah failed because the city had been rebuilt in part and surrounded by strong defenses. The Lamanites were unable to enter except through the guarded entrance and were driven back.

l: Lamanite attack on Noah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_defeated_by Nephites [at the fortified entrance] The Lamanite attack on Noah failed after the Lamanites found that the formerly weak city had been strongly fortified. Their attempts to enter or lower the banks were met with stones and arrows, causing heavy losses.

l: destruction of the Lamanite armies, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The Lamanite armies attacked fortified Nephite cities, lost chief captains and more than a thousand Lamanites, then the survivors fled into the wilderness.

l: Morianton, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Morianton, a passionate man, leads his people to claim Lehi’s land, plans northward flight after abusing a maid servant, and is killed by Teancum in battle.

l: Teancum, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Teancum is a Nephite military leader and commander, a valiant defender of liberty who serves under Moroni. He leads armies against Morianton, kills him, defeats his people, takes prisoners, and returns to Moroni’s camp. He repulses Amalickiah and the Lamanites at Bountiful, then enters Amalickiah’s tent at night and kills him with a javelin. He fortifies and defends his position, follows Moroni’s orders, and helps capture Mulek by drawing the Lamanites away. Later, with Lehi, he is left in charge of war and commands part of Moroni’s army. Finally, angered by Ammoron, he attacks and wounds him at night but is slain by Ammoron’s servants.

l: Pahoran, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Pahoran, son of Nephihah, becomes chief judge and governor over the people of Nephi in the twenty and fourth year of the reign of the judges, filling his father’s judgment-seat. Bound by oath and sacred ordinance, he is charged to judge righteously, preserve peace and freedom, protect sacred worship, support the cause of God, and bring the wicked to justice. He refuses petitions to alter the law and remains in office after the people favor the freemen. As chief judge and governor, he receives Moroni’s request to gather men for Helaman’s armies. Rebels led by Pachus drive him from the judgment-seat, forcing him to Gideon, where he gathers freemen, sends provisions to Lehi and Teancum, and asks Moroni to help reclaim Zarahemla. With Moroni he defeats the rebels, is restored to office, and helps obtain the city of Nephihah.

l: people of Morianton, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: are_restored_to land of Morianton [after covenanting to keep the peace] The people of Morianton claim part of the land of Lehi, take up arms, and flee northward after seeking to avoid Moroni's army. They are defeated, taken prisoners, and restored to their land after covenanting to keep the peace.

l: people of Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The people of Lehi flee to Moroni's camp and ask for assistance because they are not in the wrong. They are later restored to their lands and united with the people of Morianton.

l: city of Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: City in the land of Moroni by the east sea, south of Lamanite possessions; Nephites found it, but insufficient defenses let Amalickiah capture it and its fortifications after many deaths.

l: land of Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: borders land of Morianton [by the seashore] The land of Lehi lies by the seashore and borders the land of Morianton. Its people flee to Moroni for protection during the conflict.

l: land of Morianton, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: borders land of Lehi [by the seashore] The land of Morianton borders the land of Lehi by the seashore. Its people are restored to it after they covenant to keep the peace.

l: fortifications, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Fortifications are strong Lamanite-held defenses: timber works on earth ridges, high pickets, overlooking towers, and secure places atop them. Strongholds are prepared around Nephite cities; later Lamanites shelter in them, Moroni draws them out, and fortifications at Gid and Morianton are strengthened.

l: defense against the Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Defense against the Lamanites includes strongholds, armies, cleared wilderness, fortified borders, and protections that allow the Nephites to secure their cities and lands.

l: promises to Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: are_verified_for Nephites [through obedience and disobedience] The promises to Lehi are shown to be fulfilled: his children prosper when they keep the Lord's commandments and are cut off when they do not.

l: battle between Teancum and Morianton, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a battle [over the flight into the land northward] The battle begins when Morianton's stubborn people resist Moroni's army at the narrow pass. Teancum kills Morianton, defeats the army, and takes the people prisoners.

l: appointment of Pahoran, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a appointment [to the judgment-seat] Pahoran is appointed chief judge and governor after the death of his father, Nephihah. His appointment includes an oath and sacred ordinance to judge righteously and preserve peace and freedom.

l: king-men, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The king-men are a political faction and rebellion seeking to dethrone Pahoran, alter the law, and establish a king. They seek power and authority, refuse war against the Nephites during a Lamanite invasion, and cause bloodshed. After Moroni's army kills dissenters, imprisons leaders, and compels others to support liberty, the rebels rise again, drive out Pahoran, withhold provisions, possess Zarahemla, appoint a king, and ally with the king of the Lamanites.

l: freemen, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The freemen are a political faction and people supporting Pahoran, liberty, and free government by covenant. They prevail over king-men by the people’s voice, then flock to defend threatened rights, country, freedom, and avenge wrongs.

l: Moroni's army, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: executes execution of the king-men [in battle and imprisonment] Moroni's army attacks the king-men, killing or imprisoning their leaders and forcing the remainder to take up arms for their country.

l: Teancum's army, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: defeats Lamanite army [at the borders of the land Bountiful] Teancum's men repulse and harass the Lamanites, killing them until dark and camping near the borders of the land Bountiful.

l: Lamanite army, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a army [led by Amalickiah] The Lamanite army is gathered and led by Amalickiah, captures fortified Nephite cities, and is stopped by Teancum's men.

l: land of Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a land [bordering the seashore] The land of Moroni is invaded by the Lamanites, who drive out the Nephites and take possession of its city and fortifications.

l: city of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A city that receives refugees from Moroni, whose people prepare for battle; later Moroni’s army enters by night, Lamanites flee, and Moroni and Pahoran regain it without loss.

l: city of Morianton, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Morianton becomes an exceedingly stronghold as Lamanites continually bring forces and provisions; Moroni prepares to attack.

l: city of Gid, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: City Gid holds guarded Nephite prisoners until Moroni arms them, captures it by surrounding Lamanites, and strengthens its fortifications.

l: city of Mulek, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: City of Mulek, a fortified Lamanite stronghold under Jacob, is captured by Moroni after Teancum decoys its army away; Moroni gives it to Lehi. It is one of the strongest holds of the Lamanites in the land of Nephi.

l: contention over the law, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_settled_by settlement by the voice of the people [in favor of the freemen] The contention over the law concerns changing particular points and removing Pahoran as chief judge. It is settled without bloodshed by the voice of the people.

l: settlement by the voice of the people, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: favors freemen [allowing Pahoran to retain the judgment-seat] The people settle the dispute concerning Pahoran by their voice, favoring the freemen and allowing Pahoran to retain the judgment-seat.

l: Lamanite invasion, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a invasion [against Nephite lands and cities] The Lamanite invasion begins while the Nephites are divided over their government, and Amalickiah captures multiple cities before Teancum stops him.

l: execution of the king-men, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_carried_out_by Moroni's army [after authorization by the people] Moroni's army executes four thousand king-men by the sword, while leaders not slain are imprisoned and the remainder submit to the standard of liberty.

l: capture of Nephite cities, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_carried_out_by Lamanite army [under Amalickiah's leadership] Amalickiah captures the cities of Moroni, Nephihah, Lehi, Morianton, Omner, Gid, and Mulek, gaining fortified strongholds along the seashore.

l: death of Amalickiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Amalickiah’s death occurs when Teancum secretly enters his tent at night and kills him with a javelin; Lamanites discover it, and Ammoron becomes king.

l: Amalickiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Amalickiah, a king, is found dead in his own tent on the first morning of the twenty and sixth year.

l: Ammoron, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Ammoron is a descendant of Zoram, brother of Amalickiah, and king and commander of the Lamanites. Appointed after Amalickiah, he orders the Lamanites to hold captured cities and leads war against the people of Nephi without a just cause. He negotiates and disputes prisoner exchanges with Moroni and Helaman, seeking advantage while declaring the war will continue until the Nephites submit or are extinguished. He supports Lamanite forces at Cumeni with provisions and an army. While with his armies in the land of Moroni, Teancum pierces him with a javelin; Ammoron's servants kill Teancum, and Ammoron dies.

l: Jacob, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Jacob, a Zoramite with an unconquerable spirit, leads Lamanites defending Mulek, fights Teancum and Moroni, and is killed in battle.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A people who maintain cities and lands taken from the Nephites, use fortifications, retreat into Mulek, pursue Teancum, then are surrounded, defeated, and many surrender or are taken prisoner.

l: cities, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Cities are taken and held by Lamanites after bloodshed. Moroni directs Nephites to retake Mulek and strengthen nearby cities. By the end, Nephites regain every taken city, though small armies struggle to maintain them as families return home.

l: prisoners, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Prisoners are retained by Teancum as ransom for Nephite prisoners; after battle, their number exceeds those slain on both sides.

l: armies, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Armies defend borders and pursue Teancum, but coordinated Nephite commanders surround and overpower the Lamanite armies.

l: stratagem, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A military plan used by Moroni sends Teancum along the seashore while Moroni approaches Mulek, drawing Lamanites from strongholds so Moroni captures the city.

l: sons of the people of Ammon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The sons of the people of Ammon are a military force of young descendants of Laman, initially two thousand and later two thousand and sixty. Though bound by a covenant not to take up weapons against their brethren, they enter a covenant to defend the Nephites, protect their country, and fight for liberty. They call themselves Nephites and choose Helaman as leader. Before battle they are inexperienced, yet valiant, strong, truthful, sober, obedient, and continually trusting God. Joined to Antipus’s army after prisoners are sent to Zarahemla, they help secure victory at Cumeni. Later with Helaman in Manti, they suffer many wounds but remain standing; none is slain. Their steadfastness is marked by exact obedience, remembrance of the Lord God, observance of commandments, and strong faith in prophecy.

l: prisoners of the Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: are_taken_by Moroni's army [as prisoners of war] The Lamanite prisoners captured at city Gid are made to labor in strengthening the fortifications around the city. After city Gid is fortified, they are taken to city Bountiful and guarded there.

l: weapons of war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Weapons of war are cast to Nephite prisoners in city Gid, enabling silent arming; Lamanites surrender theirs, while two thousand young men take up weapons to defend their country and captured Lamanites surrender them as prisoners.

l: oath against shedding blood, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: prohibits taking up arms [against their brethren] The people of Ammon have taken an oath that they will never shed blood again. Because of this oath, they are restrained from taking up weapons even when they want to defend the Nephites.

l: covenant to defend the Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: protects liberty of the Nephites [unto the laying down of their lives] Two thousand young men enter a covenant to fight for the liberty of the Nephites, protect the land, and defend the Nephites and themselves from bondage. They covenant never to give up their liberty.

l: victory over the Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: gives_possession_of city of Mulek Moroni gains a victory over one of the greatest armies of the Lamanites and obtains possession of the city of Mulek.

l: dissensions and intrigue, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: causes dangerous circumstances [among the Nephites] Dissensions and intrigue among the Nephites cause Moroni to be absent and place the Nephites in dangerous circumstances. They enable the armies of the Lamanites on the west sea to gain ground and capture several cities.

l: liberty of the Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The two thousand young men covenant to fight for the liberty of the Nephites and never give it up.

l: prisoners, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Prisoners were central to Moroni and Ammoron’s proposed exchange: Moroni’s prisoners included no women or children, while Lamanite prisoners did; Moroni demanded a Lamanite man, wife, and children for each exchanged prisoner.

l: armies, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Armies belong to Moroni and Ammoron; in Chapter 54, each leader threatens to bring them against the other.

l: prisoner exchange, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Ammoron seeks a prisoner exchange; Moroni requires each prisoner be traded for one man, wife, and children, and Ammoron agrees to those terms.

l: land of our first inheritance, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_claimed_by Nephites [as their first inheritance] Moroni called the land of the Nephites their land of first inheritance and said that he would follow Ammoron into his own land. He also said that the Nephites would seek this land if the Lamanites continued trying to destroy them.

l: Moroni's epistle, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Moroni's epistle to Ammoron addresses war, God's justice, repentance, withdrawal, and prisoner exchange; Ammoron's reply disputes identity, fathers' wrongs, government, war, and exchange.

l: government, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The government is claimed by Ammoron for the Lamanites, whom he says the Nephites’ fathers robbed. It is later condemned for indifference to national freedom, great slothfulness, neglect, withholding provisions, and failing to strengthen armies; Moroni demands repentance and threatens destruction and opposition.

l: cause of their country, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_defended_by Nephites [as a cause of freedom] Moroni rejoiced that Pahoran was faithful to the cause of his country. Teancum was described as a true friend to liberty who had fought valiantly for his country.

l: Laman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Laman, a descendant of Laman and former servant of the king murdered by Amalickiah, helps deceive Lamanite guards with wine, causing them to become drunk.

l: Nephite prisoners, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Nephite prisoners guarded in city Gid receive weapons from Moroni, seize parts within the walls, are liberated, and join Moroni’s army.

l: wine, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Wine makes Lamanite guards believe Laman and his men escaped, then drunkenness follows; later Nephites test it on Lamanite prisoners for poison.

l: poison, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The Nephites are cautious that poison is not administered through wine. They give wine first to some Lamanite prisoners because wine poisonous to a Lamanite would also poison a Nephite.

l: saving the Nephites from destruction, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Moroni does not attack and destroy the drunken Lamanites because he delights in saving his people from destruction and does not want to bring injustice upon himself.

l: capture of city Gid, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: results_in liberation of Nephite prisoners Moroni captures city Gid by arming the Nephite prisoners, surrounding the Lamanite army, and causing the Lamanites to surrender their weapons.

l: liberation of Nephite prisoners, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: After taking possession of city Gid, Moroni causes all the Nephite prisoners there to be liberated. They join Moroni’s army and become a great strength to it.

l: Nephite victories, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: reclaim rights and privileges [for the Nephites] The Nephites begin again to be victorious and reclaim their rights and privileges. They withstand nighttime encirclement attempts and efforts to use wine against them.

l: Antipus, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Antipus leads Judea’s people and army, fortifies the city, orders Helaman near Antiparah, pursues the Lamanites, and falls by the sword in battle.

l: army of Antipus, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Antipus’s army defends Judea, pursues and surrounds the Lamanites with Helaman, defeats them, but loses Antipus and many leaders.

l: mothers, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: teach stripling Ammonites [that faith in God brings deliverance] The mothers of the two thousand young men teach them that God will deliver them if they do not doubt. The young men repeat their mothers’ words to Helaman before going into battle.

l: Judea, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a city [fortified by Antipus and his men] Judea is the city where Helaman joins Antipus and his army. Its defenders fortify it, use it as a base for watching the Lamanites, and return to it after the battle.

l: city of Antiparah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Antiparah, a city with the area’s strongest, most numerous Lamanite army, loses its people and falls into Nephite hands after its army pursues Helaman’s force.

l: Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Nephihah, populated by people gathered from three cities, is attacked, suffers slaughter, and is lost to the Lamanites as survivors flee.

l: city Cumeni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Cumeni, a city protected by Lamanites, is surrounded, deprived of provisions, yields, and remains Nephite after a repelled attack.

l: country, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The country is defended by Moroni and his men, who seek its freedom and welfare. Moroni says the people should unite to defend the country and their little ones.

l: warfare, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The warfare concerns the defense of Nephite cities against Lamanite forces. It includes fortifying cities, watching enemy movements, conducting a stratagem, pursuing armies, and capturing prisoners.

l: covenant, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: An agreement made by fathers of stripling Ammonites prohibits taking weapons of war against brethren to shed blood; Helaman initially prevents young men from breaking it, though they later defend their country.

l: provisions, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Provisions support Antipus’s army, including wives and children, with fathers of two thousand young men sending supplies. Later, food is withheld, leaving armies near starvation; Moroni demands support and vows that God will provide it, even by the sword.

l: prisoners of war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: are_sent_to Zarahemla [because there was no place to guard them] The Lamanite army surrenders as prisoners of war after being surrounded by the people of Nephi, the people of Antipus, and Helaman’s two thousand. The prisoners are sent to the land of Zarahemla because Helaman’s forces have no place to guard them.

l: battle, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A terrible battle begins as Antipus overtakes the Lamanites; Antipus falls, but Helaman returns, surrounds them, and compels surrender.

l: prisoners of war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Prisoners of war held by Helaman's forces for Zarahemla include captured Lamanites; many rebel upon hearing of approaching Lamanite armies, are slain, or escape.

l: city of Manti, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Manti, a Lamanite stronghold, was lightly guarded as its army pursued the Nephites; Gid and Teomner destroyed the guards, and the Nephites took and retained it.

l: battle with the army protecting Cumeni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A battle targets Lamanites protecting Cumeni as Helaman's forces plan a nighttime encirclement before provisions arrive.

l: capture of Antiparah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The capture of Antiparah occurs after its people leave the city and flee to other fortified cities. The city consequently falls into Nephite hands.

l: siege of Cumeni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A Nephite siege of city Cumeni: Helaman’s forces encircle and guard it, capture provisions, and compel Lamanite surrender after hope of relief fades.

l: battle at Cumeni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Battle at Cumeni: Nephites check and drive Lamanites back to Manti, retain Cumeni, preserve two thousand and sixty, but suffer a thousand slain.

l: preservation of the two thousand and sixty, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_attributed_to miraculous power of God [because of exceeding faith] Two hundred of the two thousand and sixty faint from blood loss, but all survive despite receiving many wounds. Their preservation astonishes Helaman's army while a thousand other Nephites are slain.

l: lands, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: are_in_possession_of Nephites [lands recovered from the Lamanites] The Nephites regained possession of their own lands and trusted in God for victory over them. At the end of the unit, they possessed their lands while the Lamanites had fled to the land of Nephi.

l: liberty, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_made_free_by Lord God [the liberty of the sons of Ammon] The sons of the people of Ammon stood fast in the liberty with which God had made them free. They continually remembered the Lord God and obeyed his statutes, judgments, and commandments.

l: deliverance, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_hoped_for_in Lord God [by the Nephites] The Nephites prayed for deliverance from their enemies and for strength to retain their cities, lands, possessions, wives, children, and liberty. The Lord God assured them of deliverance, and Helaman continued to trust that God would deliver them despite their weak armies.

l: stratagem to capture Manti, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: takes_possession_of city of Manti [without the shedding of blood] Helaman caused Gid and a small number of men to hide on one side of the wilderness and Teomner and others to hide on the other side. After Helaman's army drew the Lamanites away, Gid and Teomner cut off the spies, attacked the city's guards, and captured Manti; Helaman's army then returned by night and took the city without bloodshed.

l: victory, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_given_by Lord God [over the lands of the Lamanites] The Nephites obtained victory over the lands that had been taken from them and regained their cities and possessions. Helaman attributed their success to God and trusted that further deliverance would come notwithstanding the weakness of their armies.

l: people of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The people of Nephihah are attacked by Lamanites; the surviving remainder flees to join Moroni's army.

l: armies of Helaman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: belonged_to Helaman Moroni seeks to have men gathered to strengthen Helaman’s armies so they can maintain the lands Helaman regained.

l: epistle, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Moroni’s epistle, written by Helaman, requests Pahoran gather men to strengthen Helaman’s armies.

l: attack on the people of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The Lamanites attack the people of Nephihah while Moroni is preparing to battle the Lamanites.

l: slaughter of the people of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: was_caused_by Lamanites [exceedingly great] The Lamanites begin to slay the people of Nephihah with an exceedingly great slaughter.

l: loss of the city of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: affected Moroni [with exceeding sorrow] The city of Nephihah is lost to the Lamanites, causing Moroni and his chief captains to become exceedingly sorrowful, doubtful, and amazed.

l: freedom, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Freedom is the country’s cause and a privilege tied to church, Redeemer, and God. Government indifference neglects it, angering Moroni, who defends freedom and welfare over power or honor. People are urged to resist rebellion and defend it with arms against bondage; those who deny or fight it are executed according to law.

l: wickedness of the people, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: caused doubt [among Moroni and his chief captains] The wickedness of the people causes Moroni and his chief captains to doubt whether they will fall into the hands of their brethren.

l: the people, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: suffer slaughter [in great numbers] The people chose governors to manage the affairs of the war. Thousands of the people suffer and fall by the sword because of neglect, internal conflict, and the attacks of the Lamanites.

l: the war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_internal the people [among themselves] The war causes great suffering and slaughter, and the people are weakened by a war that also broke out among themselves. Moroni says they cannot successfully contend with the Lamanites until the head of the government is cleansed.

l: the slaughter, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: affects the people [thousands fallen by the sword] The slaughter among the people is great, with thousands falling by the sword. Moroni attributes much of this loss to the government's failure to provide sufficient strength and support.

l: the letter, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: contains the epistle's condemnation [directed to Pahoran and the governors] The letter is written by Moroni to Pahoran and the governors. It condemns their neglect and calls for repentance, provisions, men, and a true spirit of freedom.

l: provisions, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Provisions have not been sent sufficiently to the armies, contributing to hunger and death. Moroni demands that provisions be sent speedily to him and Helaman.

l: men, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Moroni demands that men be sent to strengthen the armies. He also asks that men be sent to Helaman so he can support the recovered parts of the country.

l: power and authority, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The king-men seek power and authority over the people, causing bloodshed and weakening the defense against the Lamanites. Moroni warns that those who seek to usurp power and authority must become extinct.

l: the sword of justice, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: hangs_over the governors [because of failure to defend the country] The sword of justice hangs over the government because it fails to defend the country and its little ones. Moroni warns that it will fall upon them and bring utter destruction unless they act.

l: neglect, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Neglect by the government causes the armies to lack strength, provisions, and support. Moroni says this neglect brings the blood and suffering of thousands upon the governors' heads.

l: slothfulness, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The slothfulness of the government leads to great neglect toward the people and armies. Moroni fears it will bring the judgments of God upon the people.

l: king over the rebels, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A king appointed over the rebels in Zarahemla writes to and allies with the Lamanite king, seeking to preserve Zarahemla and rule after conquest.

l: provisions, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Provisions are withheld by rebels, then Pahoran sends a few to Lehi and Teancum until Moroni arrives.

l: rebellion, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_caused_by rebels against Pahoran [through their efforts to take away the judgment-seat] Rebellion against Pahoran causes great iniquity and drives him from the judgment-seat. Pahoran says rebellions that cannot be resisted with words should be resisted with swords.

l: alliance, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a agreement [to maintain Zarahemla for the Lamanites] An alliance is formed between the king appointed by the rebels and the king of the Lamanites. It provides for maintaining Zarahemla and enabling the Lamanites to conquer the remainder of the land.

l: war against the Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A war against the Nephites is conducted by Lehi and Teancum according to the Spirit of God and freedom. As dissenters join and incite the Lamanites, a numerous Lamanite army comes to war against Moronihah’s army.

l: Pachus, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Pachus, king of the dissenters, drives freemen from Zarahemla, takes it, and is slain in battle by Moroni and Pahoran's armies.

l: Moronihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: commands army of Moronihah Moronihah led the people or army against whom the Lamanites came to war. His army defeated and drove the Lamanites back to their own lands.

l: land of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Moroni and Pahoran marched toward the land of Nephihah and fought and captured a large body of Lamanites on the way. After taking the city of Nephihah, Moroni marched from that land toward the land of Lehi.

l: law, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: requires_execution_of rebels [for denying freedom or fighting against the country] The law was enforced against Pachus's men and the king-men who fought against their country or refused to defend it. Regulations were later made concerning the law, and judges and chief judges were chosen.

l: thirty and first year of the reign of the judges, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: includes war between the Nephites and the Lamanites [with bloodshed, famine, and affliction] The thirty and first year included the capture of Nephihah, the death of Teancum, and the defeat and expulsion of the Lamanites. It ended with peace once more established among the people of Nephi.

l: war between the Nephites and the Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: causes affliction [through its great length] The war between the Nephites and the Lamanites had caused many years of wars, bloodshed, famine, affliction, murders, contentions, dissensions, and iniquity. Its length hardened some people and softened others, and it ended with the Lamanites driven from the land.

l: restoration of Pahoran to the judgment-seat, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: occurs_in city of Zarahemla [after Pachus is slain] The restoration of Pahoran to the judgment-seat occurred after Moroni and Pahoran defeated Pachus, slew him, and took his men prisoner.

l: capture of the city of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_accomplished_by Moroni [with Pahoran and without loss of Nephite life] The capture of the city of Nephihah was accomplished at night when Moroni's men climbed over the wall with cords and ladders. The Lamanites fled, and the city was taken without the loss of one Nephite.

l: death of Teancum, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_caused_by Ammoron [through the actions of his servants] The death of Teancum occurred after he entered the Lamanite camp and wounded Ammoron. Ammoron's servants pursued and slew him, causing Lehi and Moroni great sorrow.

l: peace in the land of Zarahemla, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_restored_by Moroni [with Pahoran] Peace in the land of Zarahemla was restored by Moroni and Pahoran after they defeated Pachus and his dissenters. Later, the people of Nephi again prospered and strengthened themselves in the land.

l: Helaman's death, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: occurs_in thirty and fifth year of the reign of the judges [at the end of the account] Helaman's death occurred in the thirty and fifth year of the reign of the judges over the people of Nephi, after the church of God had been reestablished and the people had begun to prosper.

l: Hagoth, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Hagoth, an exceedingly curious man, builds an exceedingly large ship by Bountiful and Desolation and launches it westward.

l: company of men, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A group of 5,400 men with wives and children departs Zarahemla, migrating to the land northward.

l: sacred things, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The sacred things were delivered from Helaman to Shiblon and later conferred by Shiblon upon Helaman, the son of Helaman, before Shiblon died. They were to be kept sacred and handed down from one generation to another.

l: engravings, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The engravings in Helaman’s possession were written and sent throughout the land among the children of men, except for the parts Alma had commanded not to go forth.

l: ships, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Hagoth built an exceedingly large ship, then other ships, carrying Nephites with families and provisions from the west sea to the land northward; some vanished.

l: army of Moronihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: defeats Lamanites [driving them back to their own lands] The army of Moronihah fought the Lamanites and defeated them, driving them back to their own lands with great loss.

l: migration to the land northward, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A company of five thousand four hundred men, with their wives and children, migrated from Zarahemla to the land northward. Many other people also went forth into that land in later years.

l: voyages of Hagoth's ships, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Hagoth’s ships carried Nephites, provisions, women, and children toward the land northward. The first ship returned and sailed again, while other ships sailed forth and were never heard from or had an unknown destination.

l: death of Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a death Moroni died at the end of the thirty-sixth year of the reign of the judges.

l: death of Shiblon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a death Shiblon died in the thirty-ninth year after conferring the sacred things upon Helaman, the son of Helaman.

l: defeat and retreat of the Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a military defeat The Lamanites were beaten by Moronihah’s army and driven back to their own lands, suffering great loss.

l: account of Alma, Helaman, and Shiblon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: ends account The account of Alma, Helaman his son, and Shiblon, who was his son, ended at the close of the thirty-ninth year of the reign of the judges.

l: The Book of Helaman
s: The Book of Helaman recounts Nephite political contention, war, spiritual decline, prophetic warnings, and the conversion and growing righteousness of many Lamanites before the coming of Christ. It begins after Pahoran’s death, when disputes over the judgment-seat lead to Pahoran’s murder by Kishkumen, a Lamanite invasion under Coriantumr, and Nephite recovery under Moronihah and Lehi. Helaman becomes chief judge, escapes Kishkumen’s plot through his servant, and confronts the rise of Gadianton’s secret band. Amid migrations, building, prosperity, and church growth, pride, persecution, secret combinations, and warfare repeatedly weaken the Nephites. After Helaman dies, his son Nephi succeeds him. Nephi and his brother Lehi leave political office and preach repentance among Nephites and Lamanites. Their imprisonment is followed by divine manifestations that lead thousands of Lamanites to repent, receive baptism and the Holy Spirit, see angels, abandon weapons and hatred, and yield lands to the Nephites. As the Lamanites become firm in faith, many Nephites become proud, wealthy, corrupt, and controlled by Gadianton robbers. Nephi condemns corrupt judges and warns that the Nephites will be destroyed unless they repent. He reveals the murders of Seezoram and Seantum’s guilt, receives power from God to declare judgments, and calls for famine after the people reject him. Famine brings humility and repentance; Nephi then prays for rain, peace returns, and the robbers are eliminated. Yet prosperity again produces forgetfulness, pride, dissent, and renewed robber bands. The record emphasizes that prosperity often leads people to forget the Lord, while repentance brings mercy. Samuel, a Lamanite, warns Zarahemla from its walls of destruction, famine, pestilence, and lost treasures unless the people repent and believe in Jesus Christ. He prophesies Christ’s birth, death, resurrection, and accompanying signs, including a new star, darkness, earthquakes, and opened graves. Though believers seek Nephi and are baptized, many reject Samuel, harden their hearts despite signs and miracles, and increasingly trust their own strength and wisdom.

l: The Book of Helaman, The Book of Helaman
s: The Book of Helaman is a scriptural record in The Book of Mormon, based on the records of Helaman and his sons. It recounts Nephite wars, contentions, dissensions, and prophetic teachings; records many Lamanites’ conversion and righteousness; and traces Nephite wickedness and abominations down to the coming of Christ.

l: Nephites, The Book of Helaman
s: The Nephites are a people of Nephi, governed by laws and governments established by the voice of the people. Their account centers on wars, contentions, dissensions, prosperity, repentance, corruption, and approaching destruction. Early, they contend over succession to the judgment-seat, are attacked by the Lamanites, suffer heavy losses, and then surround their attackers, receive their surrender, and recapture Zarahemla. They later face further contention, dissensions caused by pride, wars, migration, prosperity, persecution, scattering, and mixing with the Lamanites. Because of iniquity they lose nearly all the land southward and are driven into Bountiful; after repentance prompted by preaching, they regain half their possessions but cannot recover more. Their laws of Mosiah are corrupted as those choosing evil become more numerous, and the more part become hardened, impenitent, and wicked. Many join Gadianton’s bands, seek riches and gain, oppress the poor, practice murder, plunder, stealing, and false witness, and allow robbers and murderers to manage the government. Though blessed with fields, flocks, herds, wealth, safety, and peace when they cleave unto the Lord, they become proud, set their hearts on riches, reject the word of God and prophets, depend on their own strength and wisdom, and disbelieve prophecy and revelation. They are repeatedly warned that their cities, lands, and people will be destroyed unless they repent.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Helaman
s: The Lamanites are a people, including some formerly identified with Nephites and people of Ammon, who at times become mixed with Nephites and are called Lamanites. They are often numerous, possess extensive weapons and armor, and conquer the land southward and Zarahemla after dissenters stir them to anger. Under Coriantumr they invade, capture Zarahemla and other cities, then surrender after being surrounded and leave in peace. Their story also centers on conversion: after Nephi and Lehi preach, many repent, eight thousand are baptized, abandon weapons, hatred, and inherited traditions, and yield lands to the Nephites. For the most part they become more righteous than the Nephites, firm in faith, establish the church of God, preach faith and repentance, keep commandments, and live in peace and free intercourse with the Nephites while gaining riches. They experience famine and attacks, and some descendants join robbers. Though some harden their hearts and depend on their own strength and wisdom, many receive salvation, strive to bring others to truth, and are promised mercy, prolonged days, future restoration to truth, and a place among the sheep of their Redeemer.

l: Helaman, The Book of Helaman
s: Helaman, son of Helaman, is appointed by the people to the judgment-seat. He pursues robbers and secret murderers for lawful execution, judges with justice and equity, keeps God’s commandments, and prospers. He fathers Nephi and Lehi and teaches them to remember God’s commandments, repentance, Jesus Christ, and the Redeemer’s rock. He dies in the fifty-third year of the judges’ reign.

l: Jesus Christ, The Book of Helaman
s: Jesus Christ is the Son of God, the Father of heaven and earth, the Creator of all things, the Redeemer, and the only way people can be saved. Testified of by Moses and the fathers, he is represented by the serpent lifted up in the wilderness and is expected to come into the world, though some dispute that such a Christ would come. His coming marks the period to which the records extend. He will suffer and be slain for his people; his death brings about his resurrection, making resurrection and salvation possible. Through atoning blood, repentance, belief in his name, faith, and a contrite spirit, he redeems the world and the children of men from sins and spiritual death, gives eternal life, opens the gate of heaven, and brings peace. He is also the object of faith for Lamanites who refuse violence against their enemies.

l: wars, The Book of Helaman
s: Wars of the Nephites occur among the people of Nephi throughout the land. They continue through the forty-eighth year, then cease in a small degree; later, robbers, dissenters, and Lamanite descendants cause further wars. They are recorded in the Book of Helaman.

l: contentions, The Book of Helaman
s: The contentions belong to the Nephites and are internal conflicts among the people. They occur across multiple years, including the forty-sixth through forty-eighth years, begin to cease late in the forty-eighth, and give way to continual peace in the forty-ninth; refusal to heed Nephi brings division.

l: dissensions, The Book of Helaman
s: Dissensions among the Nephites arise amid contention and wars, especially in the forty-sixth year, prompting many to depart Zarahemla for the land northward.

l: prophecies of many holy prophets, The Book of Helaman
s: concern coming of Christ [before it] The prophecies of many holy prophets before the coming of Christ are included in the records of Helaman and his sons.

l: the coming of Christ, The Book of Helaman
s: The coming of Christ is a foretold event, testified of by fathers, prophets, and the holy prophets throughout generations. It is the goal toward which Helaman’s records extend and was awaited with joy. Declared as glad tidings, it was to occur after five years with signs so people could believe on his name. Though many doubted, it must shortly come, followed by his suffering and death for his people.

l: conversion of many of the Lamanites, The Book of Helaman
s: The conversion of many Lamanites, recorded in the Book of Helaman, begins as Nephi and Lehi’s preaching and spiritual manifestations convince them. They lay down weapons, hatred, and traditions, yield lands to the Nephites, bring joy to the church, and exhort the Nephites to faith and repentance.

l: righteousness of the Lamanites, The Book of Helaman
s: characterizes Lamanites The righteousness of the Lamanites is recorded in the Book of Helaman.

l: wickedness, The Book of Helaman
s: Wickedness is the great and increasing iniquity among the Nephites, recorded down to the coming of Christ. It includes pride arising from riches, oppression, violence, rejection of sacred things and prophecy, murder, robbery, adultery, contention, and secret combinations. Over successive years it grows severe, causing sorrow, affliction, weakness before the Lamanites, loss, and slaughter. The people briefly remember the Lord but forget him again, harden their hearts, reject his counsels, and strengthen in pride and evil. As they ripen in wickedness, it brings fear, curses on people, treasures, and the land, warnings to Zarahemla, Gideon, and nearby cities, and ultimately destruction.

l: Pahoran, The Book of Helaman
s: Pahoran, son of Pahoran, is appointed chief judge of the people of Nephi and holds the judgment-seat until Kishkumen murders him; his death triggers contention over succession.

l: Paanchi, The Book of Helaman
s: Paanchi, son of Pahoran, contends for the judgment-seat, grows angry when Pahoran is appointed, raises rebellion against liberty, and is tried and condemned to death.

l: Pacumeni, The Book of Helaman
s: Son of Pahoran, Pacumeni fails to obtain the judgment-seat, joins the people of Nephi, becomes chief judge after Pahoran’s death, and is killed by Coriantumr at Zarahemla’s wall.

l: Kishkumen, The Book of Helaman
s: Kishkumen is a murderer belonging to a secret band. Sent by Paanchi’s supporters, he murders Pahoran at the judgment-seat, escapes in disguise, and covenants to conceal it. He later plans to murder Helaman but is stabbed to death by Helaman’s servant. With Gadianton, he helps form and govern a band of murderers and plunderers.

l: Coriantumr, The Book of Helaman
s: Coriantumr, a mighty descendant of Zarahemla and Nephite dissenter, leads a numerous Lamanite invasion, captures Zarahemla and kills Pacumeni, advances toward Bountiful, then dies when Moronihah surrounds the Lamanites.

l: Moronihah, The Book of Helaman
s: Moronihah is a Nephite military leader and commander during a Lamanite invasion. He stations strong armies at the borders, sends Lehi against attackers near Bountiful, then directs a retreat and encirclement that recaptures Zarahemla and removes prisoners peacefully. Later, he preaches because of Nephite iniquity, leads recovery of half their possessions after repentance, maintains those lands, and establishes peace with the Lamanites.

l: Lehi, The Book of Helaman
s: Lehi, Helaman’s son and Nephi’s brother, is righteous and preaches repentance, prophecy, and God’s word among Nephites and Lamanites for the rest of his days. Driven from Jerusalem for testifying of Christ, he later commands an army that turns the Lamanites toward Zarahemla. Imprisoned with Nephi, he is surrounded by fire unharmed and shines like an angel.

l: Zarahemla, The Book of Helaman
s: Zarahemla is a great city containing Nephi’s tower and garden. Nephi and Lehi preach there, and eight thousand Lamanites and those round about are baptized unto repentance. Though much of its people practice wickedness and harden their hearts, it is spared for the righteous; without repentance, it and surrounding cities are threatened with destruction by fire from heaven.

l: people of Nephi, The Book of Helaman
s: The people of Nephi are a chosen people of the Lord, governed under judges and divided over the claims of Pahoran, Paanchi, and Pacumeni; by their voice they appoint Pahoran and later Pacumeni. At the judgment-seat they mistake five men for murderers, mourn and fast at Seezoram’s burial, and respond differently to Nephi, with some believing he is a prophet and others calling him a god. Most become proud, wicked, and hardened, practicing secret works of darkness, murderings, plunderings, and all manner of iniquities; they reject, revile, and seek to imprison Nephi. Famine and destruction lead them to remember the Lord, repent, humble themselves, and plead for relief. They then prosper, spread from sea west to sea east, and enjoy great peace, but renewed wickedness and robbers threaten them. They are warned to repent or be destroyed.

l: secret band of robbers, The Book of Helaman
s: The secret band of robbers is a combination of murderers and plunderers, formed by Kishkumen and Gadianton, bound by secrecy, covenants, signs, and words to conceal wickedness and seek murder, robbery, and power. After Kishkumen is killed, it flees into the wilderness. It spreads among the Nephites and the more wicked Lamanites, gains governmental control, and oppresses the poor and humble. Its wickedness brings destruction and wars, until the people sweep it away, make it extinct, and hide its secret plans in the earth.

l: land of Zarahemla, The Book of Helaman
s: Land containing Zarahemla as its capital city, inhabited by Nephites and surrounding regions. It is invaded by Coriantumr’s Lamanite army, then regained by Moronihah and the Nephites; it rejoices in the forty-ninth year, is obtained by Lamanites in the fifty-eighth, and later holds a wicked people mourned by Nephi.

l: the great city of Zarahemla, The Book of Helaman
s: Zarahemla, the land’s strongest hold and capital, is captured after its watch falls, occupied by Lamanites, then retaken by Nephites.

l: city of Bountiful, The Book of Helaman
s: Coriantumr marches toward the city of Bountiful with the intention of cutting through to obtain the north parts of the land. He is headed before reaching it.

l: land of Bountiful, The Book of Helaman
s: Land fortified from the west sea eastward, where Coriantumr marches toward Bountiful and Nephites under Moronihah fortify after being driven there.

l: the land northward, The Book of Helaman
s: A land receiving migrants from Zarahemla, marked by scarce timber, cement houses and cities, and large waters and rivers as people spread throughout it.

l: judgment-seat, The Book of Helaman
s: The judgment-seat is a contested place of leadership. Pahoran is appointed to it and murdered there, then Pacumeni succeeds him. Later Helaman is appointed amid contention and targeted by Kishkumen. Finally, Seezoram is found dead there, and five men are wrongly accused.

l: government, The Book of Helaman
s: has serious contention over the judgment-seat [after Pahoran's death] Serious contention and difficulty in the government prevent the Nephites from maintaining sufficient guards in the land of Zarahemla. This lack of preparation enables Coriantumr’s rapid invasion.

l: serious contention over the judgment-seat, The Book of Helaman
s: After Pahoran’s death, his sons Pahoran, Paanchi, and Pacumeni contend for the judgment-seat, dividing the people into three groups; Paanchi is condemned and Pahoran murdered.

l: appointment of Pahoran as chief judge, The Book of Helaman
s: is_by_voice_of people of Nephi Pahoran is appointed by the voice of the people to be chief judge and governor over the people of Nephi. Pacumeni unites with this decision, while Paanchi and his supporters become angry.

l: murder of Pahoran, The Book of Helaman
s: Pahoran is murdered at the judgment-seat by Kishkumen, sent by Paanchi’s supporters; Kishkumen escapes and conceals his involvement through a covenant with his band.

l: Coriantumr's invasion of Zarahemla, The Book of Helaman
s: Coriantumr leads an innumerable Lamanite army against unprepared Nephites, captures Zarahemla after killing its watch and Pacumeni, then advances until stopped.

l: battle between the Nephites and Lamanites, The Book of Helaman
s: Nephites surround Coriantumr’s retreating Lamanite army toward Zarahemla; exceedingly bloody fighting kills many, including Coriantumr.

l: death of Pacumeni, The Book of Helaman
s: is_caused_by Coriantumr [Pacumeni was smitten against the wall] Pacumeni flees before Coriantumr to the walls of Zarahemla. Coriantumr strikes him against the wall, and Pacumeni dies.

l: death of Coriantumr, The Book of Helaman
s: occurs_in battle between the Nephites and Lamanites [among many slain] Coriantumr is killed during the battle after Moronihah heads the Lamanite retreat. His death occurs while the Lamanites are surrounded by the Nephites on every side.

l: Lamanite surrender, The Book of Helaman
s: is_to Nephites [after the Lamanites were surrounded] After Coriantumr is slain and retreat is impossible in any direction, the Lamanites yield themselves into the hands of the Nephites. Moronihah then causes the captured Lamanites to depart out of the land in peace.

l: Nephite recapture of Zarahemla, The Book of Helaman
s: is_from Lamanites [after Coriantumr's invasion] After defeating and surrounding the Lamanite army, Moronihah takes possession of the city of Zarahemla again. The recapture ends the Lamanite occupation of the city.

l: weapons of war, The Book of Helaman
s: Weapons of war are laid down and buried by converted Lamanites, who abandon hatred and inherited traditions. As they become firm in faith, they refuse to take the weapons up, choosing suffering and death rather than fighting enemies.

l: prison, The Book of Helaman
s: holds five men [after they were mistakenly accused] The five men are cast into prison after the people mistakenly accuse them of murdering Seezoram. They are later released on the day of the burial, and their imprisonment contributes to their conversion.

l: Gadianton, The Book of Helaman
s: Gadianton is a leader and robber, exceedingly expert in many words and in secret murder and robbery. He leads Kishkumen’s band, promising members power and authority if they gain the judgment-seat. After Kishkumen fails to return, he causes the band’s flight through a secret wilderness way. He helps form bands of murderers and plunderers, gives secret laws, and establishes secret combinations hidden from government leaders. These works eventually cause the overthrow and near-destruction of the people of Nephi.

l: servant (Helaman's servant), The Book of Helaman
s: Helaman’s servant learns a plot to murder Helaman through disguise, confronts Kishkumen, kills him by stabbing his heart, and reports the plans and events to Helaman.

l: the people of the Nephites, The Book of Helaman
s: The Nephites, a people ruled by judges, were warned and preached repentance; they repented, prospered, and remembered Alma and Mosiah, though Gadianton later nearly destroyed them.
